Cyberattack
In computer science, a cyberattack (or cyber attack) is an attack targeted at computer systems. It occurs when there is an unauthorized action against computer infrastructure that compromises the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of its content.[1]
The rising dependence on increasingly complex and interconnected computer systems in most domains of life is the main factor that causes vulnerability to cyberattacks, since virtually all computer systems have bugs that can be exploited by attackers. Although it is impossible or impractical to create a perfectly secure system, there are many defense mechanisms that can make a system more difficult to attack, making information security a field of rapidly increasing importance in the world today.
Perpetrators of a cyberattack can be criminals, hacktivists, or states. They attempt to find weaknesses in a system, exploit them and create malware to carry out their goals, and deliver it to the targeted system. Once installed, the malware can have a variety of effects depending on its purpose. Detection of cyberattacks is often absent or delayed, especially when the malware attempts to spy on the system while remaining undiscovered. If it is discovered, the targeted organization may attempt to collect evidence about the attack, remove malware from its systems, and close the vulnerability that enabled the attack.
Cyberattacks can cause a variety of harms to targeted individuals, organizations, and governments, including significant financial losses and identity theft. They are usually illegal both as a method of crime and warfare, although correctly attributing the attack is difficult and perpetrators are rarely prosecuted.
Definitions
[edit]A cyberattack is any attempt by an individual or organization to use computers or digital systems to steal, alter, expose, disable, or destroy information, or to breach computer systems, networks, or infrastructures.[2] Definitions differ as to the type of compromise required – for example, requiring the system to produce unexpected responses or cause injury or property damage.[3] Some definitions exclude attacks carried out by non-state actors and others require the target to be a state.[4] Keeping a system secure relies on maintaining the CIA triad: confidentiality (no unauthorized access), integrity (no unauthorized modification), and availability.[5] Although availability is less important for some web-based services, it can be the most crucial aspect for industrial systems.[6]
Prevalence
[edit]In the first six months of 2017, two billion data records were stolen or impacted by cyber attacks, and ransomware payments reached US$2 billion, double that in 2016.[7] In 2020, with the increase of remote work as an effect of the COVID-19 global pandemic, cybersecurity statistics reveal a huge increase in hacked and breached data.[citation needed] The worldwide information security market is forecast to reach $170.4 billion in 2022.[8]
Vulnerability
[edit]Over time, computer systems make up an increasing portion of daily life and interactions. While the increasing complexity and connectedness of the systems increases the efficiency, power, and convenience of computer technology, it also renders the systems more vulnerable to attack and worsens the consequences of an attack, should one occur.[9]
Despite developers' goal of delivering a product that works entirely as intended, virtually all software and hardware contains bugs.[10] If a bug creates a security risk, it is called a vulnerability.[11][12][13] Patches are often released to fix identified vulnerabilities, but those that remain unknown (zero days) as well as those that have not been patched are still liable for exploitation.[14] The software vendor is not legally liable for the cost if a vulnerability is used in an attack, which creates an incentive to make cheaper but less secure software.[15] Vulnerabilities vary in their ability to be exploited by malicious actors. The most valuable allow the attacker to inject and run their own code (called malware), without the user being aware of it.[11] Without a vulnerability enabling access, the attacker cannot gain access to the system.[16]
The Vulnerability Model (VM) identifies attack patterns, threats, and valuable assets, which can be physical or intangible. It addresses security concerns like confidentiality, integrity, availability, and accountability within business, application, or infrastructure contexts.[17]
Protection
[edit]A system's architecture and design decisions play a major role in determining how safe it can be.[18] The traditional approach to improving security is the detection of systems vulnerable to attack and hardening these systems to make attacks more difficult, but it is only partially effective.[19] Formal risk assessment for compromise of highly complex and interconnected systems is impractical[20] and the related question of how much to spend on security is difficult to answer.[21] Because of the ever changing and uncertain nature of cyber-threats, risk assessment may produce scenarios that are costly or unaffordable to mitigate.[22] As of 2019[update], there are no commercially available, widely used active defense systems for protecting systems by intentionally increasing the complexity or variability of systems to make it harder to attack.[23] The cyber resilience approach, on the other hand, assumes that breaches will occur and focuses on protecting essential functionality even if parts are compromised, using approaches such as micro-segmentation, zero trust, and business continuity planning.[24]
The majority of attacks can be prevented by ensuring all software is fully patched. Nevertheless, fully patched systems are still vulnerable to exploits using zero-day vulnerabilities.[25] The highest risk of attack occurs just after a vulnerability has been publicly disclosed or a patch is released, because attackers can create exploits faster than a patch can be developed and rolled out.[26]
Software solutions aim to prevent unauthorized access and detect the intrusion of malicious software.[27] Training users can avoid cyberattacks (for example, not to click on a suspicious link or email attachment), especially those that depend on user error.[5][28] However, too many rules can cause employees to disregard them, negating any security improvement.[29] Some insider attacks can also be prevented using rules and procedures.[28] Technical solutions can prevent many causes of human error that leave data vulnerable to attackers, such as encrypting all sensitive data, preventing employees from using insecure passwords, installing antivirus software to prevent malware, and implementing a robust patching system to ensure that all devices are kept up to date.[30]
There is little evidence about the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of different cyberattack prevention measures.[27] Although attention to security can reduce the risk of attack, achieving perfect security for a complex system is impossible, and many security measures have unacceptable cost or usability downsides.[31] For example, reducing the complexity and functionality of the system is effective at reducing the attack surface.[32] Disconnecting systems from the internet is one truly effective measure against attacks, but it is rarely feasible.[20] In some jurisdictions, there are legal requirements for protecting against attacks.[33]
Attack process and types
[edit]The cyber kill chain is the process by which perpetrators carry out cyberattacks.[34]
- Reconnaissance: would-be attackers search for information about the system in order to target it. They may seek out publicly available information or carry out social engineering attacks to obtain more information about the target's systems.[34]
- Weaponization: after finding a vulnerability, attackers build an exploit to gain access, and malware to carry out the attack.[35]
- Delivery: once complete, the malware is delivered to the target.[35] Most data breaches and malware insertions are enabled by phishing, where the attacker sends a malicious communication, often an email, in an attempt to get the recipient to click on a link or attachment to deliver malware.[36] Drive-by-download does not require any clicks, only a visit to a malicious website.[36] Sometimes insiders are behind the attack and can use their credentials to bypass security.[37] Some attacks are delivered indirectly via associated companies that have a business relationship with the target. Others may be delivered by directly accessing hardware, particularly in the cases of bribery or blackmail.[35]
- Exploitation: the attacker's software is executed on the targeted system, and often creates a backdoor to enable remote control by the attacker.[35]
- Many attackers will not launch an attack right away.[38] The attacker often seeks to persist after system interruption (such as crash or restart), evade detection, and escalate privileges,[39] and secure multiple channels of communication with its controllers.[38] Other common actions include responding to remote controls and collecting and copying data to a device controlled by the attacker (data exfiltration).[39]
Activity
[edit]After the malware is installed, its activity varies greatly depending on the attacker's goals.[40] Many attackers try to eavesdrop on a system without affecting it. Although this type of malware can have unexpected side effects, it is often very difficult to detect.[41] Botnets are networks of compromised devices that can be used to send spam or carry out[42] denial-of-service attacks—flooding a system with too many requests for the system to handle at once, causing it to become unusable.[36] Attackers may also use computers to mine cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin, for their own profit.[43]
Ransomware is software used to encrypt or destroy data; attackers demand payment for the restoration of the targeted system. The advent of cryptocurrency enabling anonymous transactions has led to a dramatic increase in ransomware demands.[44]
Perpetrators and motivations
[edit]The stereotype of a hacker is an individual working for one's self. However, many cyber threats are teams of well-resourced experts.[45] "Growing revenues for cyber criminals are leading to more and more attacks, increasing professionalism and highly specialized attackers. In addition, unlike other forms of crime, cybercrime can be carried out remotely, and cyber attacks often scale well."[46] Many cyberattacks are caused or enabled by insiders, often employees who bypass security procedures to get their job done more efficiently.[47] Attackers vary widely in their skill and sophistication and well as their determination to attack a particular target, as opposed to opportunistically picking one easy to attack.[47] The skill level of the attacker determined which types of attacks they are prepared to mount.[48] The most sophisticated attackers can persist undetected on a hardened system for an extended period of time.[47]
Motivations and aims also differ. Depending whether the expected threat is passive espionage, data manipulation, or active hijacking, different mitigation methods may be needed.[41]
Software vendors and governments are mainly interested in undisclosed vulnerabilities (zero-days),[49] while organized crime groups are more interested in ready-to-use exploit kits based on known vulnerabilities,[50][51] which are much cheaper.[52] The lack of transparency in the market causes problems, such as buyers being unable to guarantee that the zero-day vulnerability was not sold to another party.[53] Both buyers and sellers advertise on the dark web and use cryptocurrency for untraceable transactions.[54][55] Because of the difficulty in writing and maintaining software that can attack a wide variety of systems, criminals found they could make more money by renting out their exploits rather than using them directly.[56]
Cybercrime as a service, where hackers sell prepacked software that can be used to cause a cyberattack, is increasingly popular as a lower risk and higher profit activity than traditional hacking.[55] A major form of this is to create a botnet of compromised devices and rent or sell it to another cybercriminal. Different botnets are equipped for different tasks such as DDOS attacks or password cracking.[57] It is also possible to buy the software used to create a botnet[58] and bots that load the purchaser's malware onto a botnet's devices.[59] DDOS as a service using botnets retained under the control of the seller is also common, and may be the first cybercrime as a service product, and can also be committed by SMS flooding on the cellular network.[60] Malware and ransomware as a service have made it possible for individuals without technical ability to carry out cyberattacks.[61]
Artificial intelligence
[edit]AI-enabled cyberattacks are increasingly considered a present and critical threat. According to NATO's technical director of cyberspace, "The number of attacks is increasing exponentially".[62] AI can also be used defensively, to preemptively find and fix vulnerabilities, and detect threats.[63]
A NATO technical director has said that AI-driven tools can dramatically enhance cyberattack capabilities—boosting stealth, speed, and scale—and may destabilize international security if offensive uses outstrip defensive adaptations.[64]
Speculatively, such hacking capabilities could be used by an AI system to break out of its local environment, generate revenue, or acquire cloud computing resources.[65]
On May 13, 2026, Lee Klarich estimated that businesses had only three to five months to get ahead of AI-driven exploits. He said companies must step up cybersecurity defenses to prepare for AI attacks.[66]
Targets and consequences
[edit]Targets of cyberattacks range from individuals to corporations and government entities.[9] Many cyberattacks are foiled or unsuccessful, but those that succeed can have devastating consequences.[20] Understanding the negative effects of cyberattacks helps organizations ensure that their prevention strategies are cost-effective.[27] One paper classifies the harm caused by cyberattacks in several domains:[67]
- Physical damage, including injury or death or destruction of property[68]
- Digital damage, such as the destruction of data or introduction of malware[68]
- Economic losses, such as those caused by disrupted operations, the cost of investigation, or regulatory fines.[68]
- Psychological harm, such as users being upset that their data has been leaked[69]
- Reputational damage, loss of reputation caused by the attack[70]
- Negative externalities to society at large, such as consumers losing access to an important service because of the attack.[71]
Consumer data
[edit]Thousands of data records are stolen from individuals every day.[9] According to a 2020 estimate, 55 percent of data breaches were caused by organized crime, 10 percent by system administrators, 10 percent by end users such as customers or employees, and 10 percent by states or state-affiliated actors.[72] Opportunistic criminals may cause data breaches—often using malware or social engineering attacks, but they will typically move on if the security is above average.[73] More organized criminals have more resources and are more focused in their targeting of particular data.[74] Both of them sell the information they obtain for financial gain.[75] Another source of data breaches are politically motivated hackers, for example Anonymous, that target particular objectives.[76] State-sponsored hackers target either citizens of their country or foreign entities, for such purposes as political repression and espionage.[77]
After a data breach, criminals make money by selling data, such as usernames, passwords, social media or customer loyalty account information, debit and credit card numbers,[75] and personal health information (see medical data breach).[78][79] This information may be used for a variety of purposes, such as spamming, obtaining products with a victim's loyalty or payment information, prescription drug fraud, insurance fraud,[80] and especially identity theft.[43] Consumer losses from a breach are usually a negative externality for the business.[81]
Critical infrastructure
[edit]Critical infrastructure is that considered most essential—such as healthcare, water supply, transport, and financial services—which has been increasingly governed by cyber-physical systems that depend on network access for their functionality.[82][83] For years, writers have warned of cataclysmic consequences of cyberattacks that have failed to materialize as of 2023[update].[84][85] These extreme scenarios could still occur, but many experts consider that it is unlikely that challenges in inflicting physical damage or spreading terror can be overcome.[84] Smaller-scale cyberattacks, sometimes resulting in interruption of essential services, regularly occur.[86]
Corporations and organizations
[edit]There is little empirical evidence of economic harm (such as reputational damage) from breaches except the direct cost[87] for such matters as legal, technical, and public relations recovery efforts.[88] Studies that have attempted to correlate cyberattacks to short-term declines in stock prices have found contradictory results, with some finding modest losses, others finding no effect, and some researchers criticizing these studies on methodological grounds. The effect on stock price may vary depending on the type of attack.[89] Some experts have argued that the evidence suggests there is not enough direct costs or reputational damage from breaches to sufficiently incentivize their prevention.[90][91]
Governments
[edit]Government websites and services are among those affected by cyberattacks.[86] Some experts hypothesize that cyberattacks weaken societal trust or trust in the government, but as of 2023[update] this notion has only limited evidence.[84]
Responses
[edit]Responding quickly to attacks is an effective way to limit the damage. The response is likely to require a wide variety of skills, from technical investigation to legal and public relations.[92] Because of the prevalence of cyberattacks, some companies plan their incident response before any attack is detected, and may designate a computer emergency response team to be prepared to handle incidents.[93][94]
Detection
[edit]Many attacks are never detected. Of those that are, the average time to discovery is 197 days.[95] Some systems can detect and flag anomalies that may indicate an attack, using such technology as antivirus, firewall, or an intrusion detection system. Once suspicious activity is suspected, investigators look for indicators of attack and indicators of compromise.[96] Discovery is quicker and more likely if the attack targets information availability (for example with a denial-of-service attack) rather than integrity (modifying data) or confidentiality (copying data without changing it).[97] State actors are more likely to keep the attack secret. Sophisticated attacks using valuable exploits are more less likely to be detected or announced – as the perpetrator wants to protect the usefulness of the exploit.[97]
Evidence collection is done immediately, prioritizing volatile evidence that is likely to be erased quickly.[98] Gathering data about the breach can facilitate later litigation or criminal prosecution,[99] but only if the data is gathered according to legal standards and the chain of custody is maintained.[100][98]
Recovery
[edit]Containing the affected system is often a high priority after an attack, and may be enacted by shutoff, isolation, use of a sandbox system to find out more about the adversary[98] patching the vulnerability, and rebuilding.[101] Once the exact way that the system was compromised is identified, there is typically only one or two technical vulnerabilities that need to be addressed in order to contain the breach and prevent it from reoccurring.[102] A penetration test can then verify that the fix is working as expected.[103] If malware is involved, the organization must investigate and close all infiltration and exfiltration vectors, as well as locate and remove all malware from its systems.[104] Containment can compromise investigation, and some tactics (such as shutting down servers) can violate the company's contractual obligations.[105] After the breach is fully contained, the company can then work on restoring all systems to operational.[106] Maintaining a backup and having tested incident response procedures are used to improve recovery.[24]
Attribution
[edit]Attributing a cyberattack is difficult, and of limited interest to companies that are targeted by cyberattacks. In contrast, secret services often have a compelling interest in finding out whether a state is behind the attack.[107] Unlike attacks carried out in person, determining the entity behind a cyberattack is difficult.[108] A further challenge in attribution of cyberattacks is the possibility of a false flag attack, where the actual perpetrator makes it appear that someone else caused the attack.[107] Every stage of the attack may leave artifacts, such as entries in log files, that can be used to help determine the attacker's goals and identity.[109] In the aftermath of an attack, investigators often begin by saving as many artifacts as they can find,[110] and then try to determine the attacker.[111] Law enforcement agencies may investigate cyber incidents[112] although the hackers responsible are rarely caught.[113]
Legality
[edit]Most states agree that cyberattacks are regulated under the laws governing the use of force in international law,[114] and therefore cyberattacks as a form of warfare are likely to violate the prohibition of aggression.[115] Therefore, they could be prosecuted as a crime of aggression.[116] There is also agreement that cyberattacks are governed by international humanitarian law,[114] and if they target civilian infrastructure, they could be prosecuted as a war crime, crime against humanity, or act of genocide.[116] International courts cannot enforce these laws without sound attribution of the attack, without which countermeasures by a state are not legal either.[117]
In many countries, cyberattacks are prosecutable under various laws aimed at cybercrime.[118] Attribution of the attack beyond reasonable doubt to the accused is also a major challenge in criminal proceedings.[119] In 2021, United Nations member states began negotiating a draft cybercrime treaty.[120]
Many jurisdictions have data breach notification laws that require organizations to notify people whose personal data has been compromised in a cyberattack.[121]

articles.title: Israel’s SPICE 1000 bombs can soon drop from F-35 fighters
articles.snippet: The Israeli air force can look forward to yet another bomb type for its F-35 fleet.
articles.full_text:
JERUSALEM — Israel’s SPICE 1000 bomb technology will soon be droppable from the country’s F-35 fighter aircraft, manufacturer Rafael Advanced Defense Systems announced on Wednesday.
The Israeli company states that the integration work is being executed as a joint initiative between Rafael and Lockheed Martin, the aircraft’s manufacturer, at Lockheed’s facilities in the United States. Development and testing are expected to conclude within a few months, according to the firm.
Following completion, the munition will be formally cleared for operational employment by the Israeli Air Force’s F-35 fleet. At a later stage, the capability is set to become available to F-35 operators worldwide.
The SPICE 1000 technology converts general-purpose and penetration warheads of 1,000 lbs into precision-capable munitions that pilots can drop from 75 miles away thanks to gliding wings on the bomb’s body. It is part of the company’s SPICE family that includes additional weight classes: the SPICE 2000 and the SPICE 250.
Rafael notes that SPICE 1000 bombs have served as a primary munition of the Israeli Air Force on F-15s and F-16s for several years, including in the recent war against Iran.
Rafael said it has sold the SPICE 1000 to several countries, but didn’t specify which. One customer emerged in December 2025 when India’s Defense Acquisition Council (DAC) approved the procurement of SPICE 1000 systems.
The Israeli Air Force maintains an active fleet of approximately fifty F-35I (“Adir”) aircrafts, and upon completion of all approved procurement processes, including the purchase of 25 aircraft this past May, Israel is projected to hold a fleet of 100 stealth fighters in total.
Tzally Greenberg is the Israel correspondent for Defense News. He has experience reporting on economic affairs as well as defense and cyber companies.

articles.title: US military must adapt as formations will be ‘hunted’ by autonomous systems, Caine says
articles.snippet: Technology, such as AI and autonomous systems, is changing the character of war, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine said.
articles.full_text:
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, emphasized that the joint force must prove readiness ahead of a conflict in a time when adversaries are becoming increasingly interconnected amid the changing character of war.
The force needs to be “clear-eyed” about the environment ahead as future conflicts will be progressively contested and defy simpler solutions, Caine said in a Wednesday keynote at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
“We have to assume from now on that our formations will be hunted by autonomous systems, jammed across the spectrum and tracked in real time,” Caine said in his speech.
“We have to transition the joint force to be prepared to fight and win our future wars by generating and delivering lethality at scale with an agile, optimized, high-low mix of combat capabilities to give the young members of the 2.8 million-member all-volunteer joint force the tools that they need before they need them,” he continued.
While calling the American military and their families the country’s “ultimate insurance policy,” Caine asserted that the joint force needs to be ready for a fight before it begins.
Even as the country’s adversaries are geographically dispersed, they are connected through sharing technology, intelligence, weapons and economic support, he said. As the military branches study past and present American battlefields, they are looking for new ways to challenge the advantage, demonstrating the necessity for readiness and investment in a range of military capabilities before a crisis begins.
Recently, Russia and Iran have deepened their military partnership with a technological feedback loop amid the Ukraine war and the conflict in the Middle East. Moscow is sending Iran upgraded munitions, satellite imagery and targeting data that have been used against American forces in the Middle East.
Tehran first supplied Russia with Shahed attack drones for use in Ukraine in 2022 and has since arranged a license to build the Iranian-designed drones on Russian territory.
“The character of war is changing, and time is of the essence,” Caine said, emphasizing how the way and speed in which countries fight is altering on the modern battlefield as artificial intelligence, cyber capabilities and autonomous systems develop.
The chairman noted that the modern battlefield today operates from the seabed to the cislunar space, highlighting that the advantage will go to whoever can see, understand, decide and act first as a learning organization.
Caine highlighted the June rescue of two Army soldiers by way of a remotely piloted Navy unmanned surface as an example of how the military is adapting and utilizing AI and autonomous tools.
He also referenced how these tools are being used to change the threat in contested electromagnetic interference environments, such as in Ukraine, with first-person view drones.
“Take it together, these examples from the Strait of Hormuz to the front lines in Ukraine show how quickly technology is changing the character of war,” he said.
Caine spotlighted that it will be young service leaders who will be the ones in charge of the subsequent conflicts in these environments and will have to be adaptive and understanding of their environment with a plethora of information.
As technology, networks and software continue to change, the need for capable and lethal leaders will not, he said. The nation can bring autonomy and better networks to the force but none of it will matter without trusted leaders that can work under pressure.
“We must move together because the window to build the force that we need is closing,” Caine said. “We can buy almost anything in life, but we cannot buy time.”
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: Air Force seeks 737 MAX for VIP airlift
articles.snippet: The aircraft would be known as the C-40 when modified for military missions, and would appear to be the first time the 737 MAX would be militarized for a government customer.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Air Force is shopping for a 737 MAX to boost its executive airlift fleet, seemingly marking the first time that planemaker Boeing’s beleaguered jetliner will be purchased for military missions.
After the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act authorized $250 million “to expand C-40 capabilities,” the Air Force intends to satisfy that requirement by buying a 737 MAX aircraft, a spokesperson for the Air Force’s Air Mobility Command told Breaking Defense. The C-40 is the Air Force’s term for earlier versions of the 737 modified for military executive airlift.
The spokesperson did not respond by press time when asked how much the procurement of the aircraft is expected to cost or its timeline for delivery. Aviation Week previously reported the Air Force’s plans to buy the MAX.
Boeing currently has several variants of the MAX in service, though the aircraft has had a troubled operational history. A pair of crashes in 2018 and 2019 prompted authorities to ground the narrowbody for over a year. A door plug subsequently fell off mid-flight from a 737 MAX in January 2024, once again sparking a crisis at Boeing over the aircraft and renewing regulatory scrutiny.
The aerospace giant is now trying to ramp up output of the MAX, a key source of cash flow. But that process, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said Wednesday, has been slower than expected.
The Air Mobility Command spokesperson did not specify which variant of the MAX the Air Force is seeking to buy, though Aviation Week noted that the command in July sought out 737-8 MAX “flight training services” in an industry solicitation. A Boeing spokesperson referred questions to the Air Force when asked about the service’s plans to procure the MAX.
The Air Force operates both the C-40 and C-32 for executive airlift, with the C-32 largely reserved for transporting “Top Five” officials — the vice president, first spouse, secretary of defense, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and secretary of state. The C-40 can also fulfill C-32 taskings, and demand for both aircraft has been high in recent years.
The defense intelligence community’s AI and cyber view forward
From AI adoption and agentic systems to Zero Trust and cyber resilience, Breaking Defense’s latest eBook brings together key reporting from DoDIIS 2026 on the technologies and strategies shaping the future of defense intelligence.
Lawmakers previously rejected the Air Force’s bid to expand the C-40 fleet under the Biden administration, Breaking Defense previously reported. At the time, the Air Force said that the C-40 could help supplement a C-32 fleet that lacked the capacity to meet a sufficient number of Top Five travel requests.
The C-32’s baseline airframe, the 757, is no longer in production, leaving the 737 as the only US-made, commercially available narrowbody jetliner that can expand executive airlift capacity. Boeing would likely be expected to handle converting the MAX aircraft for military uses, which would entail steps like installing secure communications equipment and defensive countermeasures.
Valerie Insinna contributed to this report.

articles.title: Nammo CEO warns European rupture with US risks 10-year capability gap
articles.snippet: “This industrial base among our allies is already very interconnected, so we cannot break it up,” said Morten Brandtzæg.
articles.full_text:
RAUFOSS, Norway — The CEO of one of Europe’s major ammunition and rocket motor engine producers has warned that any potential cutting off of industrial cooperation with the US risks European allies suffering a loss of capability that could take up to a decade to replace.
“If we cannot deliver AMRAAM rocket motors to Raytheon, well, none of the European F-35s” will have the weapons equipped on the fifth-generation fighter jet, Morten Brandtzæg, CEO of Norwegian manufacturer NAMMO, said Wednesday during the opening of the company’s multipurpose symposium here.
American AMRAAM-maker Raytheon is heavily dependent on NAMMO-supplied rocket motor engines for the air-to-air missile, and Brandtzæg made clear that destroying such a supply chain would be counterproductive. It would take Europe “five to ten years” to replace equivalent capabilities, he added.
“We don’t have that” amount of time, he said, appearing to refer to Russia’s war in Ukraine. “This industrial base among our allies is already very interconnected, so we cannot break it up,” he argued.
Relations between the US and Europe have been extraordinarily tense during President Donald Trump’s second administration, as Trump has repeatedly threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland and in 2024 suggested the US may not uphold NATO’s Article V commitment to collective defense for countries who did not “pay” enough into the alliance. European leaders, in turn, have publicly called on the continent to boost its domestic defense industrial base to be less reliant on the US.
But speaking to Breaking Defense and other trade media on Tuesday ahead of the symposium, Brandtzæg said that “short term [political] turbulence” cannot be allowed to ruin decades worth of industrial co-operation between Europe and the US. (Breaking Defense accepted travel and accommodation for the trip from Nammo.)
“It’s not for this industry to start running their own politics. … I support a strong cooperation among allied countries, and that includes every single NATO country and a few other countries as well,” he explained. “I think that is the way we build deterrence.”
As for Nammo, Brandtzæg said, “We are ready to step in whenever needed to do even more,” for US-based solid rocket motor production. “We have the technology and we have proven the process to work, so we are ready to step up,” including additional investment in Nammo’s Perry, Fla. production site. “We are in constant talks to help ramp up to produce more rocket motors, for missiles used by the US government,” he said.
Closer to home, Nammo recently stood up a third rocket motor production line at Raufoss, with Brandtzæg identifying additional lines as a long term target.
“We are ramping up everywhere, and we foresee to double the size of Raufoss” by 2032, he told reporters.
In the earlier stages of the Ukraine conflict, Brandtzæg called on governments to issue longer-term contracts for 155mm ammunition, on the basis that Western industry is involved in a war of capacity with Moscow.
Nammo is in “a better place” than last year, but progress is not “sufficient yet” in terms of increasing production of the shells, he told reporters.
At the symposium he went further, saying that restocking of 155mm supplies for European armies is “not there yet” as “everything we are producing is going” to Ukraine.
Nammo’s immediate plan to scale up 155mm production rests with a new, state-of-the-art facility set to open at the end of the year with production launching in 2027.
At a cost of $180 million, it takes between “two to three years to build it, and the output is just enough for seven days in Ukraine,” said Brandtzæg, of the new site.
Jack Watling, senior research fellow for applied military sciences at the British-based Royal United Services Institute think tank, said that beyond industrial planning, if Russia’s war was to stretch into a conflict directly with NATO, the “biggest challenge” for the alliance will be how to keep ammunition flowing from production to the frontline. There’s also the matter of the raw materials required.
Speaking at the symposium Wednesday, he argued against Western governments signing off new 155mm orders unless production of critical ingredients like nitrocellulose can be increased and industry can demonstrate it can preserve nitric acid supplies.
Although dependence on raw materials critical to 155mm artillery shell supplies has troubled industry throughout the Ukraine war, the situation is increasingly concerning because of infrastructure hurdles, explained Watling.
“Unless we have the high explosive to be able to go into the shelves, simply placing more orders for 155 is not going to resolve our issues because, again, if I want to set up a propellant factory somewhere, then the planning overhead [costs] alone to get permission to start building is certainly, in the UK…. [is such that it] risks making the project unprofitable.”

articles.title: Space Force’s GMTI program gets a name, with Northrop as prime: General
articles.snippet: Separately, the Space Force plans to issue the first operational contracts for space domain awareness to commercial firms “very soon,” according to Space Force Col. Timothy Tremailo.
articles.full_text:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. — The Space Force plans to begin launching a new satellite constellation that can track ground targets from orbit by 2028, according to a top service official.
Speaking with reporters at the Air & Space Forces Association conference here, Space Force Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon revealed that the Resilient Radar System-Ground, or RRS-G, program will go up “in the next two years.” The satellite system is built by Northrop Grumman, the general said.
Officials have previously discussed plans to get Ground Moving Target Indicator (GMTI)-capable birds on orbit by 2028, but until now have not disclosed the name for the specific program or the company building the satellites.
“We have a deep, operational understanding of the threats our warfighters face and are focused on delivering capability at the speed and scale required to stay ahead of them,” a statement from Northrop reads. “Any questions on specific programs are best directed to the Space Force.”
Currently ground targets are primarily tracked by sensors aboard manned and unmanned aircraft, but the Pentagon has long-sought to shift that mission, plus the tracking of aerial targets, to space-based platforms.
“The Space-Based Ground Moving Target Indicator provides resources to acquire a next-generation radar satellite system for resilient day-night, all weather detection, tracking, and imagery of ground and maritime targets,” a Space Force spokesperson told Breaking Defense. “The space-based GMTI program focuses on achieving target detection, custody, and sensor-to-shooter timelines necessary for dynamic targeting and long-range strike within highly contested and non-permissive environments.”
Gagnon, the commander of the Space Force’s Combat Forces Command, said that the service last month established its first “space-based sensing and tracking unit” dubbed the 77th Surveillance Squadron. The unit was stood up, the general explained, “to start the process of ground moving target indicator [missions], which is from the RRS-G constellation.”
The Space Force has partnered with the National Reconnaissance Office for the GMTI mission, and the service is working in parallel to develop satellites that can do the same for airborne targets. The first among many satellites for the air tracking mission, known as AMTI, will be launched this month, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said on Monday.
The Space Force plans to have an initial AMTI constellation working by 2028, following a multibillion-dollar award in May to SpaceX. It’s not clear when a GMTI constellation may be operational.
The Space Force’s baseline fiscal 2027 budget request includes $1.02 billion for GMTI procurement, while separately asking for over $7 billion in reconciliation funds for the AMTI mission. The service is also requesting roughly $1.1 billion — using combined baseline and reconciliation funding — under a separate R&D effort.
Gen. Stephen Whiting, commander of US Space Command, said today at the AMOS conference in Maui that he met with NRO officials this week to coordinate on MTI operations both in the air and on the ground.
“I think we have a good plan with the Space Force and across the department to bring those capabilities to fruition at US Space Command,” he said. “When those systems are ready to be operational, they will be presented to us, and we will be responsible for their oversight and defense of those capabilities. We’re developing the concepts of operations now for what that will look like in partnership with the other combatant commands and elements of the intelligence community that that have equities there as well.”
CASR: Coming Soon
In a separate roundtable today, Col. Timothy Trimailo, the head of the Space Force’s Commercial Space Office, said the Space Force would soon move to put commercial vendors on contract to provide space domain awareness services. Space domain awareness, or SDA, broadly refers to the ability to track and discern intent of objects in orbit.
The Space Force last year awarded pilot contracts to four companies for SDA work under the service’s Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR), which essentially aims to augment military tech with commercial capabilities in wartime. The “first step” for CASR, according to Trimailo, is to dole out contracts for operational SDA work. Those contracts will be awarded “very soon” according to the colonel.
Trimailo spoke broadly about what kinds of services CASR might pursue after the SDA mission, saying only that officials are “looking across a wide range of missions” given “a lot of demand” to examine various needs “that might be suitable” for a similar CASR arrangement.
“We’re trying to get some momentum here, and we are going to deliver operational capability through these contracts,” he said.
Theresa Hitchens contributed to this report from Maui.
UPDATED 9/17/2026 9:04 a.m. ET: This report has been updated to include additional comments from a Space Force spokesperson.

articles.title: SPACECOM needs more capabilities to target space adversaries: Whiting
articles.snippet: SPACECOM also is focusing on developing the baseline capabilities, such as space domain awareness and satellite communications, to undertake cislunar operations, said Gen. Stephen Whiting.
articles.full_text:
MAUI — US Space Command (SPACECOM) does not have all the capabilities it needs to target adversary space systems in a conflict, the command’s top officer said today.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats. Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go,” SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting told the annual Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies (AMOS) conference.
“We don’t have robust target folders like the Joint Force does in other domains,” he said.
In addition, “once a target is engaged” SPACECOM needs “real-time battlespace awareness in order to execute battle management,” he said.
Offensive actions against adversary space systems during a conflict is one function that falls under the concept of “space control,” Whiting explained.
Space control, in turn, is a “cornerstone” of US military operations given the proliferation of adversary space systems and counterspace capabilities.
“It encompasses the full spectrum of activities needed to actively contest and control the space domain, with the ultimate goal of achieving space superiority. This isn’t passive defense; it’s proactive warfighting that includes active or passive measures, kinetic or non-kinetic fires, and reversible or nonreversible effects. At its core, space control involves offensive and defensive actions collectively known as counterspace operations,” Whiting explained.
Space control, however, isn’t possible without robust space domain awareness (SDA), he said.
“Just as Sun Tzu reminded us to know the enemy, ourselves, the terrain, and the weather for complete victory, SDA integrates those multi-disciplinary insights to turn orbital data into the actionable intelligence that underpins surveillance, protection, prevention, and negation. Without it, we’re navigating blind in a contested domain where threats can emerge from any orbit or angle,” Whiting said.
“SDA truly is the bedrock of space control,” he added.
SPACECOM also is increasingly looking to fill gaps in baseline technologies ― first and foremost, SDA ― required for operations in the vast volumes of cislunar space and even farther, Whiting said.
Due to the laws of physics, objects in space farther away from the Earth are subject to differing levels of gravity, magnetic interference and solar radiation that affect how spacecraft operate.
“[A]s we expand our operations into cislunar space and beyond, we must ensure the SDA architecture is scalable—otherwise, we risk leaving deep space unmonitored and vulnerable to exploitation by our opponents,” he said.
Further, he said the US military lacks capabilities for positioning, navigation and timing; satellite communications; and “even a standard format for discussing positional states in cislunar space.”
“This represents a concern, and USSPACECOM is focused on addressing it,” Whiting said.

articles.title: Hackers claim breach of Russian election systems days before parliamentary vote
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: An anonymous hacking group claimed to have broken into computer systems connected to Russia’s election infrastructure just days before the country begins voting for a new parliament.
articles.full_text:
Hackers claim breach of Russian election systems days before parliamentary vote
An anonymous hacking group claimed to have broken into computer systems connected to Russia’s election infrastructure just days before the country begins voting for a new parliament.
The group, calling itself CikLeak, said it gained access to systems belonging to Russia’s Central Election Commission and companies involved in developing Vybory, the state-run platform used to administer elections.
The hackers claimed to have stolen internal documents, server configurations, passwords and employee communications from the commission and its contractors, including Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.
They provided the stolen material to Important Stories, an independent Russian investigative outlet that said it had authenticated the documents. However, it remains unclear how deeply the hackers penetrated the election infrastructure or whether they gained access to systems directly involved in voting or counting ballots.
“We infiltrated the infrastructure of Russia’s Central Election Commission and downloaded secret documents and developers’ internal chats,” the group claimed on its website.
CikLeak said it did not intend to disrupt voting or interfere with the work of election commissions. Instead, the group said its goal was to expose how the Russian electoral system works internally and what it described as opportunities for authorities to manipulate election results.
The hackers also published screenshots purportedly showing compromised systems and urged Russians to vote in person on the final day of the election, arguing that doing so would make manipulation more difficult.
Russia will hold elections for all 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, over three days beginning Friday. It will be the first election for the chamber since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The vote will also be the first federal election conducted using the Vybory 2.0 platform. Use of the system began this year, replacing an earlier version that had been used since the late 1990s.
Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC) had warned of growing cyber threats as voting approached.
A day before CikLeak disclosed the alleged breach, Russian election officials tested the security of the Vybory portal, remote electronic voting system and video surveillance infrastructure. The assessment identified the video surveillance system, particularly the uninterrupted transmission of its feeds, as a “weak link.”
CEC Chair Ella Pamfilova said the number of attacks targeting election systems and related infrastructure had been rising ahead of the vote.
“We have been dealing with this for years, but what is happening now is difficult to compare with anything in terms of the intensity, volume and speed of the various attacks,” Pamfilova said.
Her comments followed assurances in August that the election system was fully protected against cyberattacks. Pamfilova said information about eligible voters was updated online twice a year and stored in a closed-access system.
Russian election infrastructure has been targeted during previous votes.
During the March 2024 presidential election, hackers launched distributed denial-of-service attacks and set up phishing sites and fake Telegram channels designed to imitate official Russian services.
Rostelecom said at the time that most attacks against election infrastructure originated from Ukraine, Western Europe and North America and involved what it described as professional hacking groups.
Hackers also targeted online services belonging to United Russia, President Vladimir Putin’s political party, as well as government services in several Russian regions.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, known as HUR, later acknowledged that it was behind attacks on United Russia and Russia’s electronic voting system.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Congress eyes new support for Cyber Command after recent suicide deaths
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Congressional sources say they view the deaths of U.S. Cyber Command personnel as an inflection point, especially as the Pentagon’s appetite for cyber capabilities grows following successful contributions to high-profile missions against Iran and Venezuela.
articles.full_text:
Congress eyes new support for Cyber Command after recent suicide deaths
Congress is looking for ways to address a recent string of suicide deaths at the military’s premier digital warfighting organization, hoping to provide more mental and emotional support to personnel at a time when the tempo and duration of cyber operations have reached new heights.
Congressional sources say they view the deaths of U.S. Cyber Command personnel as an inflection point, especially as the Pentagon’s appetite for cyber capabilities grows following successful contributions to high-profile missions against Iran and Venezuela. The cluster of deaths was first reported by Bloomberg.
“It certainly shows stress on the system and that this is the time for us to react,” one congressional source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly, told Recorded Future News.
The most likely legislative vehicle to get more resources in place soon would be the annual defense policy bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which sets Pentagon policies and spending levels for national security programs. It’s typically voted on near the end of the calendar year and congressional aides will be working on the latest version while lawmakers are on the campaign trail.
Past and current military cyber operators were quick to note that it is unknown if work was a factor in the decision by these service members and civilian personnel to take their own lives.
Still, some drew similarities to beginning of the Global War on Terrorism, when drone pilots died by suicide, noting that on top of the months-long conflict with Iran and ongoing offensive and defensive cyber operations against foreign adversaries like Russia and China, digital missions now include Southern border control and counter-narcotics.
“This is something that, unfortunately, I think a lot of people … I wouldn't say saw coming but knew was going to be a possibility based on the work that goes on at Fort Meade,” according to Rep. Sarah Elfreth (D-MD), referring to the command’s headquarters, which is also home to the National Security Agency.
“Every mission across the [Defense Department] is demanding and complex. But this is a kind of a unique mission, obviously, with what happens at CYBERCOM and within the NSA,” said Elfreth, a member of the House Armed Services Committee whose district abuts the Meade fenceline.
Cyber Command and the NSA declined to comment.
The legislative angle
While the House passed its version of the NDAA earlier this year, the Senate is not expected to take up its draft before leaving town in two weeks for the campaign trail. The competing bills must be reconciled.
Staffers for the so-called “Big Four” — the chairs and ranking members of the House and Senate Armed Services committees — and others are expected to hold informal negotiations over the long upcoming break, with a final bill ready before Thanksgiving and a vote likely in December.
Staff on both panels have been briefed on the cluster of deaths, with more sessions expected in the future. Sources told Recorded Future News that the briefings could bring enough member attention to get fresh provisions included.
Elfreth, who has not been briefed on the latest incidents in detail, said she intends to push for language to expand access to mental health providers, who, due to the command’s military mission, must have security clearances themselves.
“We have a dearth of providers and access,” she said.
Elfreth also vowed to try to redefine how the Pentagon defines a suicide cluster, where the incidents take place in a short timeframe, to include civilian employees, though she admitted it would be “a bit of a Hail Mary” to accomplish that this year.
The fiscal 2024 NDAA included a provision asking DOD to study the "occupational resiliency” of the command’s Cyber Mission Force, its main operational arm.
That study, a copy of which was obtained by Recorded Future News, found “resources and programs currently available to CMF personnel are inadequate and may jeopardize long-term personnel readiness, posing unnecessary risk to the mission effectiveness of the CMF.”
The report laid out the military is taking to address the issue — including tapping senior command officials to “establish a framework to develop, manage, and assess all necessary prevention and treatment programs and procedures” — but no implementation plan has been delivered to Congress.
Demanding such a plan could draw more attention to the topic ahead of the next NDAA, according to the congressional source.
“Policy-wise I do think there are some ‘hooks’ to do stuff,” they said, using Capitol Hill slang for tacking additional oversight onto existing legislative language. “The problem is, I don't think there’s a hook to do anything funding-wise.”
Another possible route would be the next government funding bill. The House and Senate previously passed a short-term continuing resolution that keeps the government open until December 11. With just a handful of legislative days left after the midterm election, lawmakers will likely take up another stopgap measure.
One provision on the table: The House Appropriations Committee approved a fiscal 2027 defense spending bill that featured $11 million for “High Performance Team Training” at Cyber Command. It was listed second on the command’s “Unfunded Priority List” transmitted to Congress earlier this year.
The training provides “cognitive, psychological, physiological, and spiritual sustainment for high-tempo cyber operations. Without funding, burnout and force degradation will continue,” the document states.
Meanwhile, the command itself has not been idle.
Army Gen. Joshua Rudd, who helms the command and the NSA, has asked chiefs of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Air Force cyber branches to check in with him weekly for updates on their efforts around suicide.
There was also a mandatory counseling period, at least for the people in the units that were recently affected.
Burnout in highly demanding work roles has been a “major issue at the command for years. It's a consequence of the extreme operational tempo expected of the cyber mission force teams, which are essentially ‘deployed-in-place’ continually without defined rest and reset cycles,” according to Andrew Schoka, a former Army officer who served in multiple roles at Cyber Command.
“There's always new priorities and new crises to deal with, and never enough qualified personnel to support every requirement,” he added. “But beyond that, this is a leadership issue. Burning out operators is a direct result of leadership and staff that lack technical expertise in the cyber domain to properly plan, employ, and prioritize use of low-density work roles. Adding more mental health and support resources is an important step, but it doesn't address the root cause of the problem.”
Beyond Cyber Command
The recent upsurge has reverberated through the NSA, where there have also been recent suicides deaths.
Deputy Director Tim Kosiba was called to the White House last month to discuss the matter. But the conversation focused on the deaths at Cyber Command, not NSA, according to two sources with direct knowledge of the meeting. While NSA collects electronic and signals intelligence, military and civilian personnel at both entities often overlap.
Another source said the White House is “sensitive” to the issue after President Donald Trump was criticized by military families and lawmakers last month when he dismissed reports of dire conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln and said the aircraft carrier’s record-setting deployment was "not nearly long enough."
“They don’t want anyone drawing parallels with the pace they’re working people” at Fort Meade, this person said.
The reports also drew congressional scrutiny. The top Democrats on the Intelligence panels, Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia and Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, both made queries to the electronic spy agency about the resources it offers to its personnel. Neither has received a response.
“These losses are a tragedy; my heart is with their families, friends, and colleagues. I have reached out to NSA and Cyber Command for more information,” Warner said in a statement.
“The health and safety of the [intelligence community] work force is my highest priority, and I look forward to working with the Fort to ensure they have the support and resources they need to address this challenge.”
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

articles.title: Israeli contractor BlackCore trained Angolan officials in online influence operations
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: An Israeli influence-for-hire company trained Angolan government officials to run online influence operations, including by creating fake social media personas and media outlets,  researchers found.
articles.full_text:
Israeli contractor BlackCore trained Angolan officials in online influence operations
An Israeli influence-for-hire company appears to have trained Angolan government officials to run online influence operations, including creating fake social media personas and producing content designed to promote the government, according to new research.
The company, BlackCore, described itself online as “an elite influence, cyber, and technology firm built for the modern era of information warfare.” Documents obtained by researchers at the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab show BlackCore initially advertised the Angola project as an intensive four-week course covering storytelling, copywriting, traffic management and social media operations. It ultimately lasted 14 weeks and involved both training and practical operations, a final report showed.
Participants produced more than 40 pieces of content, while trainers evaluated at least 24 publications. The program also included Facebook and Instagram advertising and a TikTok campaign.
The intention was to promote what BlackCore called “positive government campaigns” and included narratives intended to portray the Angolan government “in a positive light,” rather than merely attacking government opponents, Citizen Lab senior researcher Alberto Fittarelli said.
At the center of the operation was a Facebook page for a fictitious media outlet called “Agita News,” which published its own material and linked to articles on an external website. Both are now offline.
BlackCore’s broader marketing materials advertised more aggressive capabilities, claiming it could provide clients with hundreds of fake personas, or “avatars,” across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. Its services included flooding online platforms with coordinated messages, generating engagement from real users and countering unwanted narratives with tailored content.
Determining whether an influence operation actually changed public opinion is difficult, but BlackCore appeared eager to demonstrate that its Angola operation was generating attention, researchers said.
Screenshots included in the company’s final report showed some deceptive Facebook posts receiving roughly 20,000 likes, according to Citizen Lab. Some posts that remained accessible later approached 50,000 likes — “substantial amounts in a country with an estimated six million active Facebook users.”
Citizen Lab could not independently confirm that the training took place or determine which Angolan government employees participated but the combination of internal documents and online infrastructure uncovered by researchers made it “highly likely” that the program occurred as BlackCore described it.
The researchers told Recorded Future News they found no evidence detailing how BlackCore was hired, whether the Angolan government paid the company directly or how much it cost.
Since the trainings, which likely began in February, BlackCore's websites and social media accounts have been taken offline. Citizen Lab said it was unable to find a recent contact point for the company to seek comment, and the Angolan government did not respond to Recorded Future News’ request for comment.
Broader operations
BlackCore's activities have previously drawn scrutiny from European authorities.
France's foreign-interference watchdog Viginum said in June that an information operation targeting the left-wing France Unbowed party and some of its candidates during municipal elections showed technical links to Israeli actors, including BlackCore. The campaign used websites and coordinated accounts across several social media platforms to disparage candidates and polarize political debate.
French authorities said they could not determine who commissioned the operation.
Viginum later said BlackCore was also suspected of interference activity targeting elections or political audiences in New York, Scotland, Angola and Togo.
Meta said in an August threat report that it had disrupted a coordinated network originating in Israel that targeted audiences in Angola and several other countries. According to Citizen Lab, the network was highly likely to have been operated by BlackCore.
Citizen Lab said the Angola case illustrates how governments can increasingly acquire ready-made infrastructure and expertise for covert online influence campaigns from private contractors.
BlackCore's proposal for Angola promised what it called a “professional, robust, and scalable” system for government communications, according to the researchers.
“It is not highly common” for contractors to train their clients to conduct influence operations themselves, Fittarelli told Recorded Future News, rather than running campaigns on behalf of their clients.
“Training clients to run their operations independently has been historically observed as a likely way to evade detection,” he said.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Key lawmaker suggests action on AI safety legislation will wait until 2027
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: “It's really complicated, and I wouldn't want to do something in a lame duck session to do it quickly and not get it right,” said House Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie about the FRONTIER Act.
articles.full_text:
Key lawmaker suggests action on AI safety legislation will wait until 2027
House Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie said Wednesday that he won’t pledge to a specific timeline for a committee vote on a major bipartisan AI safety bill and hinted that there likely won’t be one this year.
The legislation, known as the FRONTIER Act, is a comprehensive bill widely regarded as the best chance Congress has to put AI safety guardrails in place in the near future. Co-sponsored by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), the legislation has garnered support from OpenAI, Anthropic, important policy groups and a growing number of federal lawmakers across party lines.
Obernolte has said he wants a committee vote on the bill in November, but Guthrie appeared to oppose the idea.
“I'm not going to say that the bill is going to move,” Guthrie (R-KY) said at an event hosted by Politico in Arlington, Virginia. “It's really complicated, and I wouldn't want to do something in a lame duck session to do it quickly and not get it right.” The committee’s jurisdiction includes cybersecurity and data security.
Guthrie's comments come as the federal government, the tech industry and foreign powers debate what should happen in the short term regarding AI safety in the wake of multiple incidents of rogue AI agents launching cyberattacks.
Last week, a former Anthropic staffer quit his job and gave several interviews about his fears that AI could kill off the human race. CEOs of all the major AI companies subsequently called on lawmakers and the White House to regulate their work.
The White House has downplayed concerns and opposes additional regulation.
David Sacks, the president’s former AI czar, echoed the president’s position in an interview at Wednesday’s event. Sacks is still a White House adviser on science and technology issues and is known to have tremendous influence with the president, particularly on AI.
One possible guardrail Sacks said he would support is an idea advanced by Elon Musk for a system where AI companies test the safety of each other’s models before making them public instead of solely relying on internal testing or stronger government regulation.
“I think that's just a really interesting proposal because, again, it's marshaling the forces of competition,” Sacks said. “The other interesting thing about Elon's proposal is that Chinese companies could get on board with it.”
“There's some pre-testing period before models get released, where again the rest of the industry gets to kind of bang on those models, test those models using standard harnesses, and then find the problems before they get released.”
Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue, who also spoke at the event, said that despite his experience with some 700 rogue OpenAI agents hacking his company’s open-source platform, he believes current U.S. laws holding industry accountable for cyberattacks are all that is needed to ensure advanced AI firms are doing enough to protect against hacks.
“I’m not even sure that we need to reinvent the wheel and create new regulation because the legal system for cyber attacks is already working well today,” Delangue said.
OpenAI worked with Hugging Face on a joint forensic investigation of the incident, retained third-party auditors and said it made significant changes to its infrastructure to guard against future attacks.
Delangue did push for other reforms, saying he would like it to be mandatory for cyberattacks carried out by AI agents to be disclosed.
“I think there's a lot to do around how to create better disclosures, like do you have to disclose the full agent traces? Do you have to disclose how the models that were used for it have been trained?” Delangue said.
“There are a lot of improvements that we can make on transparency in general, that are going to be very important for the future for us to stay on top of things, understand things, and adapt our society to it [AI],” he said.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Coast Guard, FBI boarded tanker after attack by ‘foreign cyber actors’
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: U.S. personnel boarded an oil tanker in the Gulf of Mexico to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems," after an apparent cyberattack, the U.S. Coast Guard said.
articles.full_text:
Coast Guard, FBI boarded tanker after attack by ‘foreign cyber actors’
The U.S. Coast Guard said it boarded a tanker transiting the Gulf of Mexico in August after the vessel’s network was attacked by hackers.
A Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed the incident after the Wall Street Journal reported that at least two tankers headed for the U.S. were hit with cyberattacks. Bloomberg News identified one of the tankers as VL Prosperity, and Iranian government-backed news outlet Mehr said the ship lost communications for 30 hours.
The FBI did not respond to requests for comment and several other agencies directed Recorded Future News to the U.S. Coast Guard, which said officials boarded the ship to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the vessel’s network were compromised by foreign cyber actors.”
“On August 21, a highly specialized team — comprised of USCG Law Enforcement personnel, USCG Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector, and FBI Cyber Action Team operators — embarked the vessel to conduct a comprehensive cyber security boarding and investigation,” the spokesperson said.
“Currently, there are no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts.”
The U.S. Coast Guard did not respond to questions about the nature of the attack, who was potentially behind it or whether the August 21 boarding involved VL Prosperity. The Wall Street Journal said another ship was boarded on August 24.
Mehr reported that VL Prosperity was flying under a Liberian flag from a port in Egypt headed to a port in the United States when it was attacked on August 7 while transiting the Strait of Gibraltar. A crew member told Mehr that the attackers were allegedly able to increase the engine speed and disable the ship’s fuel and engine-oil tank.
The news outlet cited Russian analysts who claimed the incident was connected to the current military conflict between the U.S. and Iran but no hacking group has taken credit for the incident. Bloomberg reported that VL Prosperity is currently located off the coast of Texas.
The U.S. Coast Guard spokesperson said it is still working with port operators, vessel owners, and local maritime stakeholders to “ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption.”
One day before the alleged attack on VL Prosperity, North Carolina Ports reported a cyberattack that forced a shift to manual operations.
A spokesperson for North Carolina Ports said at the time that its IT system was “hacked by an outside actor or group” requiring them to enact a contingency plan and contact multiple state agencies as well as the U.S. Coast Guard.
Ports in the U.S., Europe and Asia have been repeatedly targeted by ransomware gangs over the last five years as many shift to incorporate digital operations. In 2024, the Port of Seattle refused to pay a ransom to cybercriminals that caused issues at the city’s airport and seaport ahead of the Labor Day holiday.
Several ports in Europe as well as large shipping companies Royal Dirkzwager and DNV were hit with ransomware in 2023 while oil companies Oiltanking and Mabanaft declared force majeure after cyberattacks in 2022 and logistics and freight forwarding giant Expeditors International similarly announced a cyberattack that crippled some of its operating systems for months.
